catalog_quote: 1.2 General remarks ... Jaane is a tone language with a high and a non-high tone level. Whether mid-tone (which occurs as well in all positions) has tonemic value must be studied later on. However, no minimal pairs have been discovered so far ... high tone spread to the right. In the following, mid-tone is not marked, whereas high (') and low (`) are always marked. This study is based on the data collected at Dolo, Diebougou and Ouan. In some cases, our data deviate from those given by Palm (2001, = P) who collected his material recently at Diebougou. Unfortunately, he only noted the singular forms. It also proved useful to add Labouret's 1958 data (= L) which was actually collected during his stay (1912-1924) ... [fn. 7, p. 241] It should be noted that in contrast to the noun stems the verbal stems do not seem to have lexical tones. ... [fn. 27, p. 253, on a form labelled 'L:'] Stress on the following syllable is marked by '.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Jaane (Dyan) is described as a tone language with two tone levels, high vs. non-high (a mid tone occurs but its phonemic status is left open; no minimal pairs found; high tone spreads rightward). The source says nothing about word stress in Jaane. The only mention of stress in the chapter is footnote 27 on p. 253, 'Stress on the following syllable is marked by \'', which explains the notation of the Lobiri comparison forms (marked 'L:'), not the Jaane data.
new_statements.exceptions: Footnote 7 (p. 241): in contrast to noun stems, verbal stems do not seem to have lexical tones. Whether mid tone is tonemic is left for later study.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (noun stems and class suffixes) in citation/elicited forms; the volume is about noun class systems, so verbs are treated only in passing. Access was through Google Books snippets: the sentences are verbatim but two separate snippet windows are joined with [..]; the full page has not been seen.
new_statements.identity_note: Jaane = Dyan (dyan1251; ISO dya); Haillot 1920 calls it 'Dian' and describes the Diébougou variety, Palm 2015 the 'parler de Diebougou', and the Miehe & Winkelmann 2007 chapter uses data from Dolo, Diébougou and Ouan. Kambou's 'Lobire' (1993, 1994), attached to dyan1251 by Glottolog, is presumably Lobiri = Lobi (lobi1245), not Dyan.
